facts.text: The hotel is at 181 Church Street in Charleston.
facts.excerpt: For well over a century, 181 Church Street has witnessed many incarnations

facts.text: Over the years, 181 Church Street housed a grocery business, a provisions company that supplied local hotels, restaurants and ships, and a bank.
facts.excerpt: from a burgeoning grocery business to a provisions company that catered to local hotels, restaurants, and ships readying to set sail. It even lived a life as a bank

facts.text: The hotel presents itself as a threshold to historic downtown Charleston.
facts.excerpt: let us be your threshold to historic downtown Charleston

facts.text: Emeline's Archive is a curated collection celebrating the Charleston Renaissance, a period from 1920 through World War II.
facts.excerpt: Emeline’s Archive celebrates the Charleston Renaissance, a time in history beginning in 1920 through World War II that fostered the city’s cultural renewal.

facts.text: The Archive includes art, books and imagery from Charleston Renaissance figures such as Elizabeth O'Neill Verner and Alice Ravenel Huger Smith.
facts.excerpt: In the curated collection you will find art, books, and inspired imagery from:

facts.text: The Gibbes Museum of Art is three blocks from the hotel.
facts.excerpt: The Gibbes Museum of Art, a short three blocks from Emeline

facts.text: The hotel runs an artist-in-residency program to connect guests with the local art scene.
facts.excerpt: we have established an artist-in-residency program to provide our guests with a personal connection to our vibrant local art scene

facts.text: The hotel sits just north of Charleston's historic open-air market.
facts.excerpt: Hotel Emeline sits just north of the historic open-air market.

facts.text: Rooms have a Crosley turntable, and the hotel has a vinyl record collection for guests to play.
facts.excerpt: With a vinyl record collection of 500 and growing, it’s only natural to settle into your room by slipping a record out of its sleeve, placing it on the Crosley turntable

facts.text: Bi-level townhouse-style 'masonette' rooms open onto the inner courtyard.
facts.excerpt: the “masonette” bi-level townhouse-style rooms opening onto the inner courtyard

facts.text: Bathrooms have walk-in rain showers and travertine floors.
facts.excerpt: state-of-the-art bathroom, with walk-in rainshower, smooth travertine underfoot

facts.text: Guests can borrow the hotel's beach cruiser bikes to ride around town.
facts.excerpt: hop on one of the hotel’s beach cruisers to pedal around town

facts.text: The hotel's restaurant, Frannie & The Fox, is built around a central wood-fired oven and opens onto an inner courtyard with a fire.
facts.excerpt: all opening onto a wide open inner courtyard with blazing fire and trellised jasmine. The menu is designed around a central wood-fired oven

facts.text: A 'foxhole' speakeasy drink window gives hidden direct access to the bar.
facts.excerpt: access the “foxhole” speakeasy drink window, a hidden direct access to the bar

facts.text: The lobby-level Keep Shop sells curated local collectibles.
facts.excerpt: The lobby-level “Keep Shop” brims with well-curated local collectibles

facts.text: The hotel is by Makeready, which worked with local maker Urban Electric on its light fixtures.
facts.excerpt: Here, they tapped local maker Urban Electric for innovative light fixtures

facts.text: A circular iron staircase leads to a mezzanine balcony overlooking the entry.
facts.excerpt: Check out the circular iron staircase leading to a mezzanine balcony overlooking the entry.

facts.text: Horse carriages can be caught right outside the hotel's front door.
facts.excerpt: You can catch a horse carriage literally out the front door

facts.text: Condé Nast Traveler named the hotel to its Hot List 2021.
facts.excerpt: Hot List 2021

facts.text: The hotel describes itself as an outpost of lighthearted luxury without pretense.
facts.excerpt: an outpost of lighthearted luxury without a hint of pretense
